chief_complaint: recurrent kidney stones and severe stomach ulcers
hpi_details: 41M with family history of gland tumors presenting with hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism) and Zollinger-Ellison gastrinoma ulcers.
ideas: He thinks his painful kidney stones and recurrent stomach ulcers are caused by a stressful job, excess stomach acid, and drinking hard or mineral-rich water.
concerns: He is worried that he has inherited the same genetic tumor condition that his family members had, which could mean dangerous growths throughout his body.
expectations: He hopes to get genetic testing and specialized imaging to check if his tumors match his relatives' condition, plus stronger medicine for his stomach pain.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes screening for the classic MEN1 triad (parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors) with biochemical testing and genetic counseling, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent kidney stones and severe stomach ulcers
Key HPI features: 41M with family history of gland tumors presenting with hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism) and Zollinger-Ellison gastrinoma ulcers.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia MEN1.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Isolated primary hyperparathyroidism without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Signs of GI bleeding or perforation from severe ulcers — a surgical emergency.
management_principles: Screen for the classic MEN1 triad with serum calcium, intact PTH, fasting gastrin, and a pituitary hormone panel (prolactin, IGF-1), and pursue genetic counseling and MEN1 mutation testing given the family history
Refer to endocrine surgery for parathyroidectomy and start a high-dose proton-pump inhibitor for gastrinoma-related ulcers while further workup proceeds
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: recurrent kidney stones and severe stomach ulcers

41M with family history of gland tumors presenting with hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism) and Zollinger-Ellison gastrinoma ulcers.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination. Evaluate for pertinent signs.
reference_soap.assessment: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1), given the combination of hypercalcemia/hyperparathyroidism, Zollinger-Ellison-type ulcers, and a family history of glandular tumors.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm hyperparathyroidism with serum calcium, albumin, and intact PTH, and evaluate for gastrinoma with fasting serum gastrin and secretin stimulation testing. Screen for other MEN1-associated tumors with a pituitary hormone panel and pancreatic/pituitary imaging. Start a high-dose proton-pump inhibitor for ulcer control while workup proceeds. Refer to endocrine surgery for parathyroidectomy and arrange genetic counseling and MEN1 mutation testing for the patient and at-risk family members.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia MEN1
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for recurrent kidney stones and severe stomach ulcers
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for endocrinology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: A hereditary syndrome causing tumors in multiple endocrine glands together — here, parathyroid hyperplasia (hypercalcemia, kidney stones) plus a gastrin-secreting pancreatic tumor (severe peptic ulcers, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).
red_flags: Signs of GI bleeding or perforation from severe ulcers — a surgical emergency

must_ask.say: How many kidney stones have you had?
How severe is your stomach pain, and have you had ulcers diagnosed before?
Does anyone in your family have glandular tumors or similar conditions?
Have you had black stools or vomited blood?
Any other hormone-related symptoms, like headaches or vision changes?

history.answer: I keep passing painful kidney stones every few months, and lately I've been having terrible burning stomach pains from severe ulcers.
My first kidney stone happened about two years ago, but this relentless burning stomach pain started around three months ago.
The stomach burning sits right in the upper middle of my abdomen, while the stone attacks hit my lower back and radiate into my groin.
The stomach ache is a severe, gnawing burning sensation that stays at about a 6 out of 10, whereas the stones cause unbearable 9 out of 10 stabbing spasms.
The kidney stones strike unpredictably every few months, but the stomach burning has become continuous day and night over the last few weeks.
Eating does not soothe the burning at all, and milk or regular antacids only calm it down for fifteen or twenty minutes before the pain flares right back up.
I've had frequent loose, watery diarrhea along with the burning, but I haven't had nausea or vomiting.
No, I have never vomited blood or coffee-ground material, and my stools have not looked black, tarry, or bloody.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
I haven't had much appetite because eating hurts my stomach, and I've unintentionally lost about 4 pounds over the last month.
I have passed three calcium kidney stones over the past two years, and each time I ended up in the emergency room needing heavy pain medications.
Whenever I pass a stone my urine turns pink or reddish with sharp spasms, but right now I don't have blood in my urine or burning when I pee.
I feel constantly fatigued and thirsty, but I haven't had severe headaches, vision changes, breast secretions, or shaky episodes from low blood sugar.
I had an upper endoscopy two months ago that showed multiple deep ulcers in my stomach and the first part of my small intestine.
I tried taking high doses of over-the-counter antacid tablets and acid-blockers, but they provided almost no lasting relief.
I don't take aspirin, ibuprofen, or any pain relievers that damage the stomach, and no specific food seems to trigger the attacks.
The gnawing stomach pain wakes me up repeatedly at night, and constantly fearing the next stone attack makes it hard to focus on my job.
I figured my stomach ulcers and kidney stones were just from a bad diet, drinking hard water, and dealing with constant stress at work.
Given my family's history with tumors, I'm really worried that these stones and ulcers mean I inherited the exact same condition.
I'm hoping to get checked for the inherited tumor syndrome that runs in my family, and to get stronger medication for this burning stomach pain.
Aside from the recurrent kidney stones and stomach ulcers, I have no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, or other chronic conditions.
I had a hospital stay last year for shock wave lithotripsy to break up a large kidney stone, but I've never had surgery on my abdomen.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, only over-the-counter antacid chews when the burning gets intolerable.
I have no known allergies to any medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink one or two beers socially once or twice a month, and I have avoided alcohol completely since this stomach pain began.
I work full-time as an accountant, and I live with my wife and our two young children.
My father had parathyroid surgery for high blood calcium and died from a neuroendocrine tumor, and my paternal uncle also suffered from gland tumors and severe ulcers.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Alert, oriented male appearing mildly uncomfortable due to abdominal ache, but in no acute toxic distress.
Pink palpebral conjunctivae without pallor; non-icteric sclerae bilaterally.
Visual fields are fully intact to confrontation bilaterally; pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light with no bitemporal hemianopsia.
No cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy noted.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and contour, non-tender, with no palpable nodules.
Normal S1 and S2 heard at a regular rate and rhythm, with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear breath sounds heard symmetrically across all lung fields without crackles or wheezes.
Flat, symmetrical abdomen without surgical scars, distension, or visible pulsations.
Normoactive bowel sounds present throughout all four quadrants without bruits.
Moderate tenderness elicited on deep palpation of the epigastrium; no involuntary guarding, rigidity, or palpable masses.
No rebound tenderness noted anywhere across the abdomen.
No Murphy's sign; no tenderness over the right upper quadrant or gallbladder bed.
No tenderness elicited upon percussion over the costovertebral angles bilaterally.
Normal skin turgor and texture without rashes, facial angiofibromas, or subcutaneous lipomas.
